What are the criteria of asphyxia that causes hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)?
A cord pH below 7.0 (base deficit of 12 or more), a low Apgar score at 10 minutes, early encephalopathy and dysfunction of several organs.
When does the asphyxial insult most commonly occur?
Before or during labour (in about 90% of cases).
What are the features of Sarnat stage 1 HIE?
The baby is hyperalert with normal tone and no seizures; the outcome is good.
What are the features of Sarnat stage 2 HIE?
The baby is lethargic and hypotonic with weak reflexes, and seizures are common.
What are the features of Sarnat stage 3 HIE?
Coma, flaccidity, absent reflexes and frequent seizures; the outcome is poor.

How are fluids managed after asphyxia?
Fluids are restricted, to about 40–60 ml/kg/day on day 1.
Why is hyperthermia avoided in HIE?
Every degree above normal adds to the brain injury.
What are the criteria for therapeutic hypothermia?
A baby of 36 weeks or more, with asphyxia and moderate or severe HIE, within 6 hours of birth.
What are the target temperature and duration of cooling?
A core temperature of 33.5 °C for 72 hours.

What are the bad prognostic signs in HIE?
A severe stage, seizures lasting more than 24 hours, a burst-suppression EEG and injury of the basal ganglia on MRI.
